tagline: Forested bluffs and a former wagon road lead toward Neah Bay
intro: SR 112 winds between forested hills and coastal viewpoints on the northern Olympic Peninsula. State of Washington Tourism lists a two-hour drive and highlights beach access, outdoor recreation and opportunities to learn about the Makah Tribe. The route became a National Scenic Byway in 2000.

A trail along the strait became a wagon road in the 1920s, with a Milwaukee Road logging railroad later built alongside it. The county road entered the state system in 1937; a road connecting Neah Bay to the highway was completed by 1953. A proposed extension down the outer coast met opposition: conservationists and Supreme Court Justice William O. Douglas joined a 22-mile protest hike in 1958. Further protests followed federal approval in 1964, and the coastal extension was canceled. The highway became SR 112 in 1964, and state scenic-byway designation came in 1967.

Driving west from US 101, cross the Elwha River gorge and follow the former railroad grade through the rural plain near Joyce. Beyond Twin Beach, coastal bluffs and creek-crossing hairpins lead toward Pysht. The road turns inland along the Pysht and Clallam river valleys before returning to the coast at Clallam Bay and Sekiu. SR 112 ends at the Makah Reservation boundary; the road continues as Bayview Avenue to Neah Bay, the tourism byway’s endpoint.

moments.title: Salt Creek Recreation Area
moments.text: The 196-acre park lies near Joyce on SR 112. Two surviving gun casemates give Salt Creek Recreation Area a history beyond its beaches and trails. The site began as the Striped Peak Military Reservation in 1941, became Camp Hayden in 1942 and was renamed Fort Hayden in 1944. Battery 131 held two former Navy 16-inch guns linked by a large magazine bunker. The park now provides access to Tongue Point, sandy beaches, upland forests and rocky bluffs. State of Washington Tourism identifies low tide as the time to see marine life in the tidepools.

moments.title: Clallam Bay
moments.text: The town sits where the Clallam River enters the bay, with Sekiu on the western side. Clallam Bay grew from an 1880s steamboat stop into a mill town in 1890. When the mill burned two years later, barrel-making for West Clallam Bay’s tanning extract became its main industry. The maritime story also reaches Slip Point, where a light filled the gap between Cape Flattery and Ediz Hook. Its original fog house and tower were replaced in 1951. The keeper’s house survives in use by the local sheriff’s department, along with concrete footings from the catwalk that once connected the quarters to the light.

moments.title: Makah Museum, Neah Bay
moments.text: Canoes, basketry and whaling and fishing gear are among the objects interpreted at the Makah Museum in Neah Bay. Also called the Makah Cultural and Research Center, the museum houses artifacts from the Ozette village, partly buried by a mudslide around 1750. Tribal chairman Edward Eugene Claplanhoo led its creation, and it opened in 1979 after the site was unearthed. The displays include a replica long house alongside the archaeological collection.

practical: Makah Museum, Neah Bay: For outdoor activities on reservation land, display a Makah Recreation Permit in your vehicle. (checked 2026-10-11)
